meta.name: Dogo Argentino
meta.tagline: The Dogo Argentino is a powerful, all-white Argentine hunting and guardian breed, recognized by the AKC in 2020. About one in four Dogos in the only published prevalence study (811 BAER-tested U.S. Dogos) were deaf in at least one ear, so insist on a BAER-tested puppy — and know that this is a breed for experienced owners.
meta.excerpt: The Dogo Argentino is a devoted, athletic guardian bred to hunt boar and puma, and a breed for experienced owners. Here's what to know about BAER hearing tests, exercise, costs and where the breed is restricted.
meta.meta_description: Dogo Argentino guide: a guardian-minded AKC Working breed, why BAER hearing tests matter, exercise needs, real costs, and where the breed is restricted.
meta.title_tag: Dogo Argentino: Temperament, Care, Health, Cost
meta.quick_answer: The Dogo Argentino is a large working dog, weighing 80–100 lbs and living 9–15 years. Plan on 60–90+ min of exercise a day. Grooming is low; training is moderate (experienced handler). It is best with older children and supervision. It is not recommended for first-time owners.

hero.alt: Adult white Dogo Argentino sitting calmly on a backyard lawn

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What Is a Dogo Argentino?
intro.html:
The Dogo Argentino is a large, all-white big-game hunting dog from the province of Córdoba in central Argentina. Dr. Antonio Nores Martínez, with his brother Agustín, developed it from the now-extinct Old Fighting Dog of Córdoba crossed with breeds including the Great Dane, Pointer, Bull Terrier, Boxer, Bulldog, Pyrenean Mastiff, Irish Wolfhound and Spanish Mastiff, and Antonio set down the first standard in 1928 (Dogo Argentino Club of America; AKC). The breed was made to hunt wild boar, peccaries and pumas — and, in the words of today’s standard, to protect family and property.

Argentina’s kennel federation recognized the Dogo in 1964, and the FCI accepted it in 1973 as the first Argentine breed. The AKC granted full recognition in January 2020 and placed it in the Working Group (Dogo Argentino Club of America; AKC).

Two realities belong up front. In the only published prevalence study, covering 811 BAER-tested U.S. Dogos, about one in four were deaf in one or both ears (Strain, 2021), so a BAER hearing test on the puppy itself is essential. And this is a powerful, high-drive dog that the AKC says does especially well with an experienced owner. The breed is also banned or restricted in some countries — see the legal checklist below.

appearance.label: Physical
appearance.heading: What does a Dogo Argentino look like?
appearance.html:
Big, heavily muscled and athletic. The standard sets tight height limits — 24–26½ inches for males and 24–25½ inches for females — and a dog outside them is disqualified. The AKC lists weight at 80–100 lbs; the standard itself gives approximate weights of 88–100 lbs for males and 88–95 lbs for females (DACA breed standard; AKC).

The coat is short, smooth and entirely white. The only tolerated markings are a single dark patch on the head (on the skull, one ear or around one eye) covering no more than 10% of the head, and very small dark spots on the ears. Blue eyes, a nose that isn’t black, long hair, more than one patch on the head and any black spot on the body are all disqualifications (DACA breed standard).

Dogos are sometimes mistaken for pit bulls, but they are a separate and much larger breed: the Dogo’s minimum height of 24 inches is above the top of the UKC’s 18–21 inch range for American Pit Bull Terrier males (UKC).

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: What is the temperament of a Dogo Argentino?
temperament.html:
The standard describes a strong, tenacious and rustic dog created to protect family and property and to hunt large game — a faithful companion at home and in the field, and above all courageous (DACA breed standard). At home, that usually looks like a devoted, affectionate family dog with a serious protective streak: the AKC scores the breed 5 out of 5 for both affection with family and watchdog/protective nature.

The AKC also notes the breed’s intelligence and strong prey drive, and says a Dogo will do especially well with an experienced owner. Its trait scores flag supervision around young children (3 of 5) and with other dogs (3 of 5), and put energy at the top of the scale (5 of 5) (AKC).

In practice, that means cats and small pets need careful, supervised management, if they are compatible at all; introductions to other dogs should be slow and deliberate; and socialization with people should continue well past puppyhood so the dog’s protectiveness stays in proportion. The AKC scores openness to strangers at 4 of 5, so a well-socialized Dogo is often polite with visitors — but it is still a guardian breed, not a greeter.

mikes_take.label: A Realistic Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Thinking About a Dogo Argentino
mikes_take.html:
The Dogo is an impressive animal — athletic, devoted and genuinely affectionate with its own people. But I’d only recommend one to someone who has already lived with a large, driven breed. This is a big-game hunting dog with a guardian’s instincts and 80–100 lbs of muscle behind them, and the AKC’s own advice is that it does best with an experienced owner.

I have three non-negotiables. First, a BAER hearing test on the specific puppy you’re buying, not just its parents: in a study of 811 BAER-tested U.S. Dogos, deafness in one ear (20%) was nearly four times as common as deafness in both (5%), and a puppy that’s deaf in one ear looks and acts normal (Strain, 2021). Second, skip anyone selling “rare” blue-eyed or spotted Dogos — both are disqualifications, and blue-eyed dogs trended toward more deafness in that same study. Third, ask for the parents’ health results through the parent club’s CHIC program.

The other thing I’d flag is logistics. Before you commit, check your lease, HOA and homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, and if you might ever move abroad, know that the UK bans the breed and Australia prohibits importing it. Then plan for a securely fenced yard and a real daily commitment to exercise and training for a decade or more.

care.label: Daily Life
care.heading: How much exercise and grooming does a Dogo Argentino need?
care.html:
Exercise

The AKC rates the Dogo’s energy at the top of its scale. Plan on 60–90+ minutes of real activity a day — long walks, hiking, structured fetch or flirt-pole play and scent work — plus short training sessions for the mind. Hold off on hard running and jumping until your vet says a young dog’s joints are ready. Because this is a prey-driven hunting breed (AKC), a tall, secure fence matters, and a Dogo shouldn’t be trusted off leash in unfenced areas.

Training & Socialization

Dogos are intelligent, and the AKC scores them highly trainable, but their size and drive raise the stakes of any training gap. Start a positive-reinforcement puppy class early and prioritize loose-leash walking, a recall practiced on a long line, a reliable “leave it” and calm settling. Keep socializing with people, places and handling through adolescence and beyond, and introduce other dogs slowly.

Grooming

The short white coat needs little more than weekly brushing, occasional baths and regular nail trims — the AKC puts grooming needs at 1 of 5 — but it sheds more than many people expect (AKC shedding score: 4 of 5). Ask your vet about sun protection for a white-coated dog that spends long hours outdoors.

Living With Hearing Loss

If your Dogo is deaf in one or both ears, train with hand signals from day one, keep the dog leashed or fenced outdoors, and wake it gently with a touch rather than startling it.

health.label: Wellness
health.heading: What health problems are common in the Dogo Argentino?
health.html:
The AKC calls the Dogo a generally healthy dog with few genetic problems and lists a lifespan of 9–15 years. The Dogo Argentino Club of America (DACA), the breed’s AKC parent club, has run a CHIC health program since 2021: BAER hearing, hip and cardiac evaluations are required, plus one elective test (DACA). Its 2020 health statement goes further on hearing, requiring breeders to BAER-test all breeding stock and every litter they produce (DACA, 2020).

ConditionWhat It Means
Congenital DeafnessThe breed’s best-documented health problem. Of 811 U.S. Dogos BAER-tested, 74.2% heard normally in both ears, 20.4% were deaf in one ear and 5.4% were deaf in both — about 26% overall. Dogs without a head patch had higher rates, and blue-eyed dogs trended higher, though that group was too small to be conclusive (Strain, 2021). Only a BAER test reliably detects deafness in one ear.
Hip DysplasiaAbnormal hip development that leads to arthritis and pain. DACA’s CHIC program requires an OFA or PennHIP hip evaluation on breeding dogs (DACA).
Heart DiseaseDACA’s CHIC program requires a cardiac exam at 12 months or older performed by a veterinary cardiologist (DACA). OFA’s CHIC listing for the breed accepts either an advanced (cardiologist, with echo) or a basic cardiac exam at 12 months or older (OFA), so ask which was done and see the report.
Elbows, Thyroid and EyesThe CHIC elective tests: breeders choose at least one of an OFA elbow evaluation, an autoimmune thyroiditis test through an OFA-approved lab, a CAER eye exam by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, or DNA banking with the CHIC repository (DACA).
Disproportionate DwarfismDACA has recently added disproportionate dwarfism to the genetic testing in its health program (DACA). Ask whether the parents have been tested.

Ask breeders for: BAER results for the exact puppy you’re buying (both ears), plus each parent’s BAER, OFA or PennHIP hip and cardiologist cardiac results, at least one CHIC elective test, and any dwarfism test results. A CHIC number shows the required tests were done and the results made public — not that every result was normal (OFA), so read the results themselves.

cost.label: Budget
cost.heading: How much does a Dogo Argentino cost?
cost.html:
DACA doesn’t publish price guidance, so the figures below are estimated ranges from Rover’s 2026 all-breed cost survey rather than Dogo-specific quotes. Expect a large, high-energy dog to land toward the upper end: Rover notes that small-breed adults can cost as much as 63% less per year than large- to giant-breed adults.

ExpenseFirst YearAnnual (ongoing)
Adoption fee (shelter or breed rescue)$50–$500—
Or puppy from a breeder (all-breed range)$675–$4,440—
Other up-front costs: spay/neuter, microchip, first exam, vaccines, supplies, license$1,145–$4,150—
Routine care: food, treats, vet visits, preventatives, dental care, training, insurance, toys$1,460–$6,745 (puppy year)$1,930–$5,305
Estimated Total$2,655–$11,395 (adopting)
$3,280–$15,335 (breeder)		$1,930–$5,305

How the totals were built: first-year totals add Rover’s 2026 up-front and puppy-year ranges, which overlap slightly (the first bag of food, the first preventatives), so they lean high. For insurance, the average U.S. accident-and-illness premium for dogs was $836 a year in 2025 (NAPHIA); quotes vary with breed, size and location.

Dogo-specific costs to plan for: DACA requires BAER testing on every litter, so a reputable breeder’s price should already include the puppy’s hearing test; home or renters liability coverage, since some insurers decline certain breeds (Triple-I); and a tall, secure fence.

right_for_you.label: Fit Assessment
right_for_you.heading: Is a Dogo Argentino Right for You?
good_fit: Experienced owners who have raised and trained a large, driven or protective breed
Active households ready for 60–90+ minutes of exercise and training every day
Homes with a tall, secure fence and time for socialization that continues through adolescence
Buyers willing to wait for a breeder who BAER-tests every puppy and health-tests the parents
Families with older, dog-savvy children and adults who will supervise every interaction
not_fit: First-time dog owners — the AKC says the breed does best with an experienced owner
Homes with cats, small pets or other dogs that you can't reliably keep separated
Anyone who can't physically control an 80–100 lb dog on leash
Renters or owners whose lease, HOA or insurer restricts large guardian breeds, or who live in (or may move to) the UK or Australia
Anyone wanting a low-shedding dog or a laid-back couch companion

finding.label: Next Steps
finding.heading: Where can you find a Dogo Argentino puppy or rescue?
finding.html:
Step One: Check the Law and Your Insurer

Rules change often, so treat this as a starting checklist rather than legal advice.

  • The UK. The Dogo Argentino is one of the banned types, and whether a dog counts depends on what it looks like rather than its papers (GOV.UK).
  • Australia. Importing a Dogo Argentino is prohibited (Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956).
  • United States. There is no federal ban. Denver’s Breed-Restricted Permit applies only to the American Pit Bull Terrier, American Staffordshire Terrier and Staffordshire Bull Terrier (City and County of Denver), and Florida law bars local breed-specific rules (Laws of Florida 2023-253), although HOAs there can still restrict breeds (Miami Herald). Individual towns, landlords and insurers can set their own rules, so check your city code, lease, HOA rules and your insurer’s breed list before you commit.
  • Rescues check too. DC Dogos Rescue considers local, state and residential breed-specific rules when deciding on adopters (DC Dogos Rescue).

Buying from a Breeder

The AKC parent club is the Dogo Argentino Club of America, which publishes a code of ethics and a list of regional clubs. It doesn’t run a public breeder directory, so the AKC breeder referral contacts are a good place to start. Ask for the puppy’s own BAER report, each parent’s CHIC results (BAER, hips, cardiologist cardiac exam and an elective test), a chance to meet the mother, and a written contract that includes taking the dog back if you can’t keep it. Walk away from blue-eyed or spotted puppies sold as “rare,” missing BAER reports, or pressure to send a deposit before you’ve met the dogs.

Before you pay anyone, read our guides to finding a responsible breeder and spotting puppy scams.

Rescue

DC Dogos Rescue, the rescue listed on the AKC’s Dogo page, places dogs in the continental U.S. only, requires a home check, and notes that applications can take one to three weeks or longer; its adoption page doesn’t list a fee (DC Dogos Rescue). An adult rescue may come with a known hearing status and a track record with people and other dogs. Our guide to adopting vs buying a dog walks through the trade-offs.

faq.q: Is the Dogo Argentino banned in the US?
faq.a: There is no federal ban in the United States. Denver's breed-restricted permit covers only the American Pit Bull Terrier, American Staffordshire Terrier and Staffordshire Bull Terrier, and Florida law bars local breed-specific rules. Towns, HOAs, landlords and insurers can still set their own rules. Outside the U.S., the Dogo is a banned type in the UK, and Australia prohibits importing it.

Many are, at least in one ear. In a study of 811 BAER-tested U.S. Dogos, about 26% had congenital deafness: 20.4% in one ear and 5.4% in both (Strain, 2021). Dogs without a head patch were more often affected. Because a puppy deaf in one ear looks normal, ask for a BAER report on the puppy itself; the parent club requires BAER testing on all breeding stock and litters.

faq.q: Are Dogo Argentinos good family dogs?
faq.a: In experienced hands, they can be devoted, affectionate family dogs: the AKC scores them 5 of 5 for affection with family and for protective nature. The AKC also scores them 3 of 5 with young children and advises supervision, and notes a strong prey drive. They suit active adults and older, dog-savvy children better than first-time owners or homes with toddlers.

faq.q: Is a Dogo Argentino a pit bull?
faq.a: No. The Dogo is a separate Argentine breed developed from the extinct Old Fighting Dog of Córdoba and several other breeds, accepted by the FCI in 1973 and recognized by the AKC in 2020. It is also much larger: the Dogo standard's minimum height is 24 inches, above the UKC's 18–21 inch range for American Pit Bull Terrier males. Some laws still restrict both breeds; the UK bans each as a separate type.

faq.q: How much does a Dogo Argentino cost?
faq.a: The parent club doesn't publish price guidance. As an all-breed benchmark, Rover's 2026 survey puts breeder prices at $675–$4,440 and adoption fees at $50–$500, with adult dogs costing $1,930–$5,305 a year to keep. Large dogs tend to land toward the upper end. A reputable breeder's price should include the puppy's BAER hearing test.

faq.q: Are Dogo Argentinos good with other dogs?
faq.a: It varies, and supervision is the rule. The AKC scores the breed 3 of 5 with other dogs and notes a strong prey drive, which also matters around cats and small pets. Slow, controlled introductions and ongoing management work better than dog parks.
